'''''Buddleja coriacea''''' is a variable species [[endemic]] to the high Andes from the [[Cordillera Blanca]] in Peru to [[Lake Titicaca]] in Bolivia. It is also native to Ecuador.<ref name=IUCN/> It grows on dry to semi-humid rocky soils at elevations of 3,000–4,350 m,<ref name=Norman>Norman, E. M. (2000). Buddlejaceae. ''Flora Neotropica 81''. New York Botanical Garden, USA</ref> where temperatures range from −3° to 15° [[Celsius|C.]] and the winds are both strong and persistent.<ref name="Jøker">Jøker, D., Cruz, N., Morales, M., & Rojas, E. (2002). Buddleja coriacea Remy ''Seed leaflet''. No. 54, Jan. 2002. BASFOR, Danido Forest Seed Centre, Humleback, Denmark.</ref><ref name=Arica>Arica, D. (2013). Buddleja coriacea - 'Colle', 'Kishuara'. ''Algunas Especies Forestales nativas Para la Zona Altoandina.'' (''Some native forest species for the High Andes''). CONDESAN (Consorcio para el Desarrollo Sostenible de la Ecorregion Andina), Lima, Peru.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=www.infoandina.org |url=http://www.infoandina.org/sites/default/files/recursos/DArica3_1.pdf}}</ref>{{dead link|date=July 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} The species was first named and described by [[Jules Rémy|Rémy]] in 1847.<ref name=Norman/>

==Description==
''Buddleja coriacea'' typically makes a densely crowned, sprawling [[trioecious]] shrub or tree, branching almost at ground level. Usually growing to less than 4 m in height in the wild, it can occasionally reach 12 m, with stems up to 40 cm in diameter; the bark is fissured.<ref name="Jøker"/><ref name=Norman/> The species is chiefly distinguished by its small, thick, leathery leaves, 1–4  cm long by 0.5–1.5 cm wide, with 3–4 mm [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s. The upper surfaces of the leaves are dark-green and glabrous, contrasting with the undersides which are covered in a [[cinnamon]]-brown [[indumentum]]. The scented [[inflorescence]]s comprise 3–8 pairs of head-like cymes, 0.9–1.2 cm in diameter, of 8–12 flowers, the [[corolla (botany)|corollas]] 4.5–6 mm in length, deep yellow to orange-yellow, becoming orange-red with age. Flowering occurs throughout the year, but most commonly between December and June. [[Ploidy]]: ''2n'' = 76 (tetraploid).<ref name=Norman/>

==Cultivation==
''Buddleja coriacea'' is cultivated in the high Andes as a field windbreak, as a source of humus for soil improvement, and as high quality, rotproof timber for use in building construction and manufacture of agricultural tools.<ref name=Arica/> The shrub was introduced to horticulture in the UK circa 1994, and specimens are held as part of the [[NCCPG]] national collection at the [[Longstock Park]] Nursery, near [[Stockbridge, Hampshire|Stockbridge]].<ref name=Moore>Moore, P. (2012). ''Buddleja List 2011-2012 Longstock Park Nursery''. Longstock Park, UK.</ref> 
Although not entirely hardy in the UK, the shrub can survive most winters with a modicum of protection; overwinter waterlogging regarded as a greater danger to the plant. The shrub has never been known to flower in the UK owing to either the insufficient intensity or duration of sunlight. [[Hardiness zone|Hardiness]]: [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]] zone 9.<ref name=Stuart>Stuart, D. (2006). ''Buddlejas''. Timber Press, Oregon, USA. {{ISBN|978-0-88192-688-0}}</ref>

==Hybrids==
The species is believed to commonly hybridize with [[Buddleja montana|''B. montana'']] and [[Buddleja incana|''B. incana'']] in the wild.<ref name=Norman/>
